title: Voyager 1 Is About to Reach One Light-Day From Earth
summary:
When NASA launched Voyager 1 in 1977, it was expected to last just five years. Almost 50 years later, the spacecraft is still working, and it is about to reach an amazing milestone.

Voyager 1 travels at about 38,000 miles per hour. It has already traveled more than 15.8 billion miles through space. If it keeps going on its current path, it will be one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026. A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, about 16 billion miles. Voyager 1 will be the first human-made object ever to reach that distance.

The spacecraft's first job was to study Jupiter and Saturn. It flew past both giant planets and sent back detailed pictures and information about their rings, moons and atmospheres. Because Voyager 1 was still in good shape, NASA decided to send it on into deep space.

In 2012, Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space. That is the region far beyond the Sun, where the Sun's energy becomes very weak.

Voyager 1 still sends information back to Earth, but its nuclear power source is slowly making less electricity. To save energy, NASA engineers have been turning off some of its science instruments. On April 17, 2026, they shut off an instrument that measured charged particles. It had helped scientists understand how space weather changes far from Earth. Voyager 1 now has two instruments still working.

NASA is also looking for other ways to help the spacecraft last longer as its power weakens. If those efforts work, Voyager 1 could keep collecting valuable information for many more years.
why_it_matters: Voyager 1 shows how carefully built machines can keep exploring for decades, sending back information from places no other spacecraft has reached.

background_read: Voyager 1 is a robotic space probe, a spacecraft with no people on board that is controlled by engineers on Earth.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe, so scientists use the distance it travels in a set time to describe huge distances in space.
Spacecraft that travel far from the Sun cannot rely on sunlight for power, so Voyager 1 uses a nuclear power source that slowly weakens over time.
Signals from Voyager 1 take a very long time to reach Earth because it is so far away, and huge antennas on Earth listen for them.
